- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes (e.g., 78–80 range), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “rebound” or “mean reversion” effect.
- Model exhibits persistent downward bias in the final 5–10 days of the 30-day forecast, especially when true values show a clear downward trend.
- Model often fails to adjust for recent downward momentum — if the last 5–7 days of history show falling prices, forecast still tends to hold or slightly rise.
- Model underestimates the magnitude of downward corrections after spikes — e.g., after 80+ prices, model often predicts 70–75, but true drops to 60–65.
- Model overreacts to recent volatility — if history shows rapid swings, forecast tends to over-smooth or over-forecast direction, missing the “mean reversion” to prior levels.
- Model tends to ignore the “tail” of the price distribution — especially when true values show a sharp drop in the last 5–7 days, model still predicts a plateau or slight rise.
- Model often fails to account for seasonal or calendar-based patterns — e.g., if true values drop sharply in late January, model doesn’t adjust unless recent history shows similar pattern.
- Model underestimates the impact of policy or market events — if a policy change or market shock occurred recently, model doesn’t adjust forecast downward unless it’s explicitly modeled.
- Model exhibits “lagged” behavior — it takes 3–5 days to adjust to new trend, leading to persistent overestimation in early forecast days.
